name: Sunekos

card.summary: Italian injectable that mixes hyaluronic acid with amino acids as a skin 'biorevitalising' booster; supported mainly by small manufacturer-linked trials.
card.aka: Sunekos 200, Sunekos 1200, Sunekos Performa, amino-acid booster
card.note: Few published trials; most registered studies are small and have no posted results in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Sunekos is an injectable that combines hyaluronic acid with amino acids in an alkaline solution, offered in clinics as a skin booster for photoaging, under-eye circles and body skin laxity. The idea is that amino acids supply building blocks for the skin's collagen and elastin.

The published evidence found is thin: one multicenter cellulite study of 46 women, plus registered small studies on face, under-eyes and body.
quick.mechanism: Clinicians inject the mixture into or beneath the dermis at several points. Proponents say the amino acids support fibroblast activity; the published research located does not test this mechanism directly.
quick.risks: The cellulite study assessed safety alongside efficacy. As with other injectables, local reactions such as swelling and bruising are expected; long-term safety data are limited.

lead: Sunekos is a commercially available mixture of hyaluronic acid and amino acids in an alkaline solution, injected for skin aesthetics.[1] Registered studies have evaluated it for face photoaging, the area around the eyes and skin laxity of the inner thighs, knees and arms.[2][3][4][5]
A 2026 prospective multicenter study evaluated the mixture for cellulite (edematous fibrosclerotic panniculopathy) in 46 women using an injection technique, reporting on efficacy and safety.[1]

paras: The 2026 cellulite study was prospective and multicenter, enrolling 46 women with stage I to early stage disease and assessing both efficacy and safety.[1]

Registered studies include a twelve-person half-face comparison of two injection techniques for photoaging,[2] a 25-person intradermal photoaging study,[5] a 22-person under-eye dark circle study,[4] and a 24-person study on inner thighs, knees and arms.[3] Posted results were not available in the sources reviewed.
